note: The sentence ledger of the four customer-journey pages WP-72 wrote (docs/wave8-contracts.md, sections 8.2 and 11; plan 5.3). Each sentence maps to one claim (C-nn), one existing page with a heading (path#heading), or one decision (W8-nn); a title or heading that states no fact about WE is a label (seven words at most). A question for the founder to put to WE states no fact about WE: it maps to the page that already covers its topic, or to W8-25, the journey contract, where the program pages are silent. The template's own sentences (the note under the hero, the section headings and the checklist note) are WP-71's and are traced in its ledger. tests/unit/wp-72/ enumerates the sentences from the content files, fails on one with no mapping and on a mapping with no sentence, and runs the claims denylist over all of them. The resources hub (src/pages/resources/index.astro) is the fifth document. Its own copy (page strings, group titles and intros, the strip) is held strictly; each item title and description is read from the page the item links to and is mapped to that page's file, so a page another package adds changes the list without editing this file (tests/unit/wp-72/resources.test.ts). The file has no fetches: it quotes no outside source.

sentences.text: The founder journey
The path from an application to a working team, in five steps, with a page for each stage.
It states no durations and promises no outcomes.
Which of these five steps am I at today, and what would the next one ask of me?
Which page below explains the step I am least sure about?
What would I want to know from WE before I send an application?
The path starts with an application and runs through the same five steps the program pages describe.
The pages below take those steps from three angles: what happens after you apply, what you see and decide along the way, and what you can prepare.
WE makes no promise of funding.
Start with what happens after you apply.
Pass it on
If you know a founder who is weighing a program like this one, you can pass this page on.
Copy the address from your browser and send it however you usually send a link.
An organization that helps or equips founders may send WE an enquiry through the partner enquiry form.
Sending one creates no partnership, no referral arrangement and no commitment on either side.
What happens after you apply
What follows an application, in the order the program pages give it, and the questions to put to WE at each step.
No durations and no outcomes.
What will the written scope name as in and out for my company?
Which service lines does my company need, and what will each one not cover?
Which roles does the scope call for, and what will each seat work on?
How will I see the goal and the artifacts of each cycle?
What should I bring to a review so that I can decide what the next cycle holds?
How does the agreement set out scaling seats up or down by notice?
First, WE reviews the application
WE reviews each application.
WE replies to the email address you give.
WE does not state a response time on this site.
A clear no is as useful to you as a yes.
How WE decides lists what an application is read for and what WE does not decide.
Then you and WE agree the scope
If the idea fits, WE and the founder choose which service lines the company needs and what each one will and will not cover.
The scope is written down in an agreement, so both companies work from the same page.
WE shares the written agreement before you commit to anything, and you should read it with your own counsel.
What this page leaves to you
This page repeats only what the program pages already say.
Where they are silent, the questions below are for you to put to WE.
WE makes no promise of funding.
Next, read your first months, in order.
The full path is on How the program works.
Your first months, in order
The five program steps from the founder's side: what you see, what you decide and what to ask, in order.
No durations and no promised outcomes.
Which of these steps do I want to understand better before I apply?
What would I want to see written down at each step?
This page follows the five program steps from the founder's side.
For each step it says what you see, what you decide and what you can ask WE.
WE makes no promise of funding.
Apply
You see a short application that asks only what WE needs to judge fit.
You decide how to tell WE about the idea, the founder and the stage you are at.
What does WE need to see in an application to judge fit for my idea?
How will WE tell me if my idea is not a fit?
Agree the scope
You see the scope written down in an agreement, so both companies work from the same page.
You and WE choose which service lines the company needs and what each one will and will not cover.
You decide whether to commit, and you should read the written agreement with your own counsel first.
Which service lines will the scope name, and what will each one not cover?
How will the agreement describe how WE is paid?
Seat your team
You see dedicated offshore seats for the roles the scope calls for.
The seats work only on your company, and WE steers them.
You do not recruit, contract or manage the people in the seats.
Which roles does the scope call for, and what will each seat work on?
Which subcontractors will WE manage for my company, if any?
Work in focused cycles
You see a stated goal and a visible set of artifacts for each cycle.
You and WE agree the goal of each cycle in a short written plan.
The work in progress is open to you at any time.
What is the goal of the next cycle, and which artifacts will it produce?
How does WE use its ANDROID Ops loop to decide what a cycle contains?
Review and decide
At each review you see what exists now, what changed and what is next.
You decide what the next cycle holds, and you can scale seats up or down by notice as the agreement sets out.
What changed since the last review, and what is still open?
Which seats should change, and how does the agreement set out the notice?
Where to go next
Use the onboarding checklist to prepare for each step.
When you are ready, apply to the program.
Onboarding checklist
A checklist to read before and after you apply, built from the program steps and the library.
It is guidance, so use the parts that help.
Which of these items do I already have, and which could I start before I apply?
Write the problem on one page: who has it, what they do today and what you have seen.
Plan your conversations with people who have the problem, and keep your solution out of them.
Decide what the first release leaves out, and write the cut line down.
Read the two fit lists and judge your own fit before you apply.
Read what the application asks, so your answers describe the idea, the founder and the stage you are at.
Note the service lines you think the company needs, and what you expect each one not to cover.
Sketch the roles your team needs and how many seats each role takes.
Plan to read the written agreement with your own counsel before you commit.
Choose the goal you would give a first cycle, so the plan has something to start from.
Choose the numbers you would track, and test them in the metrics calculator.
When you start to prepare evidence for investors, work through the investor readiness checklist.

The founder journey
The path from an application to a working team, in five steps, with a page for each stage.
It states no durations and promises no outcomes.
How the program works
From application to a working team: apply, agree the scope, seat the team, work in reviewed cycles and decide what comes next.
Fully remote.
Validate the problem
Test whether a real, painful problem exists before you write code: a problem brief, honest interviews and a written decision.
One-page problem brief
A single-page template that states the problem, the customer, the evidence and the next test, so a team can agree on what it is solving before it builds.
Team Composer
Sketch the roles your SaaS team needs and how many seats each role takes.
No sign-up, no price, nothing stored.
Carry the sketch to the application.
FAQ
Short, plain answers about World Enterprise Incubator: what a seat is, how the remote model works, what WE does not do, and how to apply.
Build and ship v1
Build the first release in short cycles, keep a release checklist, review against the cut line and put it in front of a small group.
MVP cut-line worksheet
A worksheet for deciding which features belong in a first release and which wait, using the customer job, the riskiest assumption and a clear cut line.
SaaS Metrics Calculator
Enter one month of SaaS numbers to see net new MRR, churn, quick ratio, CAC payback, LTV to CAC and runway.
Every formula is shown.
Nothing leaves the page.
Earn your first customers
Win your first customers with personal outreach, a scoped pilot, fast onboarding and a conversation log that records why people said yes or no.
Glossary
Plain definitions of the funding, finance, product, legal and security terms early-stage SaaS founders meet, plus the words WE uses.
Fundability and investor readiness
What investor readiness means for an early SaaS company, a twelve-statement self-check, and four guides: checklist, data room, SAFE and investor updates.
Investor readiness checklist
Twelve statements that show a SaaS company has its evidence in order, each with the artifact that proves it and where to start if it is missing.
Seed data room checklist
A checklist of the documents a seed-stage company usually organizes before investor due diligence, grouped by folder, with an owner and status for each.
Evidence Room Builder
A checklist of the records an early SaaS company gathers before due diligence.
Filter by stage, tick items off, then print the list or copy it as Markdown.
Weekly investor update template
A short, repeatable update format that reports progress, decisions, risks and requests in plain language, without inflating results.
SAFEs in plain language
A plain-language explanation of the SAFE, a short contract for future shares: how it works, the terms to know and questions for your own lawyer.
Customer interview guide
A script and note sheet for discovery interviews that surface real behavior and past events instead of opinions about your idea.
Security baseline checklist
A first-year security checklist for early-stage SaaS teams covering access, code, data, vendors and response, written as questions about your own product.
Founder playbooks
Five step-by-step playbooks for building a SaaS company, from validating the problem to repeatable growth, each with artifacts and common mistakes.
Design the product
Turn a validated problem into a version-one design: the shortest path to value, a written cut line and the decisions you will defer.
Build repeatable growth
Define your metrics in writing, run one channel long enough to learn, fix leaks before adding traffic and turn the results into a monthly review.
The seed data room
What a seed-stage data room is, the folders it usually holds, and how to keep it organized and current without exposing anything it should not.
Investor updates
How to write a short, consistent progress update for investors, advisers and supporters, with a fixed structure and honest numbers.
Founder tools
Three tools for an early SaaS founder: sketch a team, work out your monthly metrics, and build an evidence checklist.
Each one runs in your browser.
Four designed reports with methodology, limitations and sources: security, accessibility, staffing models and SaaS metrics, for founders building software.
Security baseline for year one
What a first-year SaaS security baseline can draw from OWASP ASVS, NIST SSDF and the AICPA Trust Services Criteria, and how to sequence the work.
Accessibility at launch
A source-based reading of WCAG 2.2, Section508.gov and the DOJ ADA Title II web rule, with a labelled analysis of why accessibility belongs in launch scope.
Team, agency or freelancers
A criteria-based decision framework for choosing between a dedicated team, an agency and freelancers, with the legal basics that apply to each.
SaaS metrics definitions
Definitions and a formula appendix for MRR, ARR, churn, NRR, CAC and LTV, drawn from public references, with a reporting discipline and no benchmarks.
Insights
Practical, sourced articles on validating, building, growing and preparing a SaaS company, written by World Enterprise Editorial.
Who WE builds with
What WE asks of a founder, what a founder keeps doing, and the evidence WE looks for before scoping a dedicated team.
Criteria, not stories.
